faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.intro: Didn't find the answer to your question? Please <contact>contact us</contact>.

q1.question: What are webinars?
q1.answer:
Our webinars are online training sessions on current topics in data protection law and sometimes on topics from law in the digital sphere.

We normally hold the webinars of our Data Protection Academy live. The duration of the webinars varies, also depending on questions from members. Most webinars last between 30 and 60 minutes.

The webinars are held by Martin Steiger, attorney-at-law and co-founder of Datenschutzpartner, or by another specialist, possibly together with other participants.

All webinars are recorded. During your membership of the Data Protection Academy, you can access the recordings of all previous events. You can also access slides and other materials.

Information about individual webinars can be found in the Data Protection Academy dashboard.

q2.question: What are News & Questions?
q2.answer:
“News & Questions” is a regular event of our Data Protection Academy. The event consists of the “News” and “Questions” sections.

In the “News” section, we inform members of the Data Protection Academy about relevant updates in data protection law and related topics.

In the “Questions” section, members of the Data Protection Academy can ask their own questions and receive helpful answers from a specialist, for example from Martin Steiger, attorney-at-law and co-founder of Datenschutzpartner.

Members of the Data Protection Academy can not only ask their own questions, but also hear the answers to questions from other members.

With “News & Questions”, members of the Data Protection Academy can improve their knowledge in three ways: through the news, through answers to their own questions, and through the answers to other members' questions.

“News & Questions” usually lasts around 30 minutes, depending on the number of questions and news items, sometimes a little shorter or longer.

For “News & Questions”, members of the Data Protection Academy take part in a live webinar together with other members. Questions can be asked live via the Q&A function or in advance using the member form.

“News & Questions” is recorded and published for members of the Data Protection Academy. The publication includes, among other things, the collected questions.

The recordings and materials for all events can be found in the Data Protection Academy dashboard.

“News & Questions” replaced the former “Legal Sessions” in summer 2025.

q3.question: How will I find out about new content and dates?
q3.answer: Information about content and dates can be found in the Data Protection Academy dashboard. We will also inform you by email about new content and dates.

q4.question: How do I get access to recordings and other content?
q4.answer:
You can find all available recordings and other content, such as checklists, in the Data Protection Academy dashboard.

We also publish most content for members of the Data Protection Academy on our website. To access member content, you must log in.

q5.question: Can earlier events be accessed?
q5.answer: Yes, during an active membership of our Data Protection Academy, all previous events with all available recordings, slides and other materials can be accessed.

q6.question: How practice-oriented is the content?
q6.answer:
Our Data Protection Academy is aimed at everyone who has to implement data protection law or wants to stay up to date. We try to make our offering as practice-oriented as possible and focus on implementation in organizations and companies.

Members of our Data Protection Academy have the opportunity, in particular, to ask their own questions in our “News & Questions”.

q7.question: Are there any special technical requirements?
q7.answer:
No, there are no special technical requirements for taking part in our Data Protection Academy.

We primarily use the video conferencing service Zoom. To participate, a current browser on a Mac or PC, on an iPhone or iPad, or on other current devices is sufficient. However, it is optimal if you use the Zoom app.

(Apart from that, you will of course need a working internet connection and a way to hear the webinar audio.)

q8.question: How can I use Zoom without the app?
q8.answer:
When you open the web link to a Zoom event of the Data Protection Academy in your browser, you will be asked whether you want to open the Zoom app.

If you cancel or decline, you can click “Join from your browser” (or similar) at the bottom. This allows you to use Zoom in your browser without needing the Zoom app.

q9.question: Why am I asked for my name and email address before a webinar?
q9.answer:
We primarily use the video conferencing service Zoom to hold webinars and other events online.

In some cases, before participating in such Data Protection Academy events, you will be asked for your name and email address.

We do not need this information. You can therefore enter any details.

q10.question: How can I access the transcript for recordings?
q10.answer:
For newer Data Protection Academy events whose recordings are available as video, you can access the transcript of the event in the bottom right of the video window by clicking the icon with paper and a magnifying glass.

You can search for text in the transcript and jump to the relevant passages. You can also jump forward and backward using the timestamps in the transcript.

The transcript is generated automatically. The spoken word is therefore authoritative in terms of content.

q11.question: How can I activate subtitles for recordings?
q11.answer:
For newer Data Protection Academy events whose recordings are available as video, you can activate the subtitles in the bottom right of the video window by clicking the “CC” icon (or deactivate them if they are active).

The activated subtitles appear at the bottom of the video window.

The subtitles are generated automatically. The spoken word is therefore authoritative in terms of content.

q12.question: Why do you use the informal form of address?
q12.answer:
We aspire to be your data protection partner. An informal culture fits that very well. We therefore switched from the initial, somewhat distant formal address to the collegial informal form.

You may of course address us formally if you wish. In that case, we will also address you formally again.

q13.question: How can I pay for my membership?
q13.answer:
You can pay for your membership of our Data Protection Academy by credit card or invoice.

You will receive your invoice as a PDF file by email. The payment term is 10 days. For credit card payments, we use the payment service Stripe.

q14.question: What happens if an appointment is cancelled?
q14.answer: Data Protection Academy appointments that are cancelled, for example due to illness or technical reasons, will be rescheduled where possible.

q15.question: Does my membership renew automatically?
q15.answer:
Yes, your membership of our Data Protection Academy renews automatically.

In particular, we inform you under “My Account” about the term of your membership. You can cancel your membership at any time effective at the end of the current term.

euRepresentation.label: Data protection representation in the EU

q1.question: What is the European General Data Protection Regulation?
q1.answer:
With its General Data Protection Regulation, abbreviated GDPR, the European Union (EU) has harmonized and tightened its data protection law. The GDPR focuses on enforcing existing data protection law.

The GDPR entered into force on 24 May 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018 after a two-year transition period. The GDPR applies directly in all EU Member States and is also applicable in the member states of the European Economic Area (EEA), including the Principality of Liechtenstein.

In addition, the GDPR applies at least in part to many companies and organizations in Switzerland, even though Switzerland is not a member state of the EU or the EEA. Under the market location principle, the GDPR applies in part to the processing of personal data outside the EU and EEA.

In the EU, the GDPR is referred to as Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

q2.question: What is the difference between the DSGVO and the GDPR?
q2.answer: The English name of the European General Data Protection Regulation, abbreviated DSGVO in German, is General Data Protection Regulation, abbreviated GDPR. There is no difference between the DSGVO and the GDPR other than the language.

q3.question: What happens if you do not comply with the GDPR?
q3.answer:
Anyone who violates the GDPR may be punished with fines of up to EUR 20 million or up to 4 percent of worldwide turnover. These are the maximum penalties, particularly with regard to American companies such as Google or Meta. The data protection supervisory authorities may also request information and conduct investigations, among other things.

Swiss companies and organizations must also expect to be penalized. The GDPR provides that penalties must be dissuasive, proportionate and effective. Irrespective of any penalty, even the costs caused by proceedings due to an alleged GDPR violation can be painful, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

In addition, many contracts provide that applicable law or expressly the GDPR must be complied with. One example is data processing agreements, as required by the GDPR. Anyone who does not comply with the GDPR breaches such contracts and must expect, for example, claims for damages from contractual partners.

Furthermore, the rights of data subjects are strengthened by the GDPR, meaning that they can also defend themselves. There are concerns, among other things, that data protection warning letters may become more common.

q4.question: Why does the GDPR apply to many companies in Switzerland?
q4.answer:
With the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the European Union (EU) introduces the market location principle into data protection law:

The GDPR applies to the processing of personal data of all persons located in the European Economic Area (EEA). The EEA comprises the EU Member States as well as the Principality of Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.

To protect these persons not only in the EEA but worldwide, the GDPR generally also applies when such data is processed in countries outside the EEA, in so-called third countries (Art. 3 para. 2 GDPR). From the EU's perspective, Switzerland is such a third country.

q5.question: Under what conditions does the market location principle apply to companies in Switzerland?
q5.answer:
Companies in Switzerland whose offering is directed at persons in the EU or the EEA must comply with the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) with respect to such persons. Free offerings such as e-books, newsletters and white papers (“freebies”) for persons in the EU and EEA are also expressly covered.

In addition, the GDPR applies to companies in Switzerland that monitor the behavior of persons in the EU or EEA, for example by analyzing the activities of visitors in an app or on a website (profiling and tracking). Anyone who uses Google Analytics on a Swiss website, for example, may thereby be subject to the GDPR.

Swiss companies and organizations that are subject to the GDPR require an EU data protection representative. You can use our questionnaire to find out whether you need a data protection representative in the EU.

q6.question: Are there exceptions?
q6.answer:
Swiss companies that must comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) exceptionally do not need a data protection representative in the EU if the following three conditions are met:

1. The data processing is only occasional, and
2. there is no extensive processing of particularly sensitive data, and
3. taking into account the nature, circumstances, scope and purposes of the processing, the data processing is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

We advise against relying on these exceptions.

q7.question: What are the tasks of an EU data protection representative?
q7.answer:
The EU data protection representative is an additional point of contact for supervisory authorities and data subjects for all requests in connection with ensuring compliance with the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Art. 27 para. 4 GDPR).

The EU data protection representative can also be imagined as a “mailbox” in the EU that authorities and data subjects in the European Economic Area (EEA) can use.

q8.question: What requirements must an EU data protection representative meet?
q8.answer:
An EU data protection representative must be a legal or natural person established in an EU Member State. The establishment must be located in one of the EU Member States where data subjects are located. We ensure that you can order our offer online, but that the order is made in writing.

The EU data protection representative for our clients is our subsidiary VGS Datenschutzpartner GmbH, based in Hamburg. The data protection representation applies, starting from Germany, to the entire EU and to the entire EEA, including the Principality of Liechtenstein. Anyone subject to the GDPR under the market location principle almost always also processes data of data subjects in Germany.

q9.question: To what extent does the data protection representative in the EU bear responsibility?
q9.answer:
The liability and responsibility of companies in Switzerland for compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) are neither excluded nor reduced by appointing a data protection representative in the EU. The companies concerned remain themselves fully responsible for compliance with the GDPR, which includes, among other things, appointing a data protection representative in the EU (Art. 27 para. 5 GDPR).

The data protection representative in the EU may be instructed by the data protection supervisory authorities to provide all information required for the performance of the supervisory authorities' tasks. If the data protection representative in the EU does not have the necessary information, it must obtain it from the represented company.

q10.question: Is one EU data protection representative sufficient per group or corporate group?
q10.answer:
No, one EU data protection representative per group or corporate group is not sufficient.

According to Art. 27 para. 1 GDPR, every individual controller and every individual processor within the scope of the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) must appoint an EU data protection representative.

In principle, the individual legal entities or comparable legal units are considered individual controllers or processors.

q11.question: What happens if the tasks and requirements for the data protection representative in the EU change?
q11.answer: If the tasks and requirements for the EU data protection representative in the EU change, we will adapt our offering accordingly.

q12.question: What kinds of requests should be expected?
q12.answer: Supervisory authorities and data subjects may contact the EU data protection representative at any time. In this way, data subjects may, for example, exercise their rights of access, data portability, erasure and objection. Supervisory authorities may, for example, forward complaints from data subjects or request information about compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

q13.question: How many requests should be expected?
q13.answer:
Experience shows that most controllers have to expect few or no requests. Controllers who are reachable for data subjects are normally contacted directly and not via the EU data protection representative.

Data protection supervisory authorities normally contact the EU data protection representative. However, such requests are usually self-provoked, whether through notifications of data breaches or requests from data subjects that were not answered directly.

As a rule, we only forward requests in connection with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Obvious email advertising (spam), for example, is not forwarded.

q14.question: How and where must the EU data protection representative be mentioned?
q14.answer:
The EU data protection representative must be mentioned in particular in the respective privacy policy and in the record of processing activities. However, mention in the legal notice is not required.

Our clients will find the required details and sample wording for their privacy policies in our guide for EU data protection representation.

Anyone using our privacy policy generator automatically receives, where the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies, a privacy policy with suitable text for the EU data protection representative.

q15.question: Does the EU data protection representative need the record of processing activities?
q15.answer: The EU data protection representative does not need the record of processing activities pursuant to Art. 30 GDPR as standard. However, as part of their data protection obligations, controllers must keep a record of processing activities and also be able to provide the record of processing activities to the EU data protection representative promptly if needed.

q16.question: Must a telephone number be provided for the EU data protection representative?
q16.answer: No, Art. 27 GDPR as the legal basis for the EU data protection representative does not require a telephone number to be provided.

euRepQuestionnaire.title: EU data protection representation questionnaire
euRepQuestionnaire.intro: Answer the following questions one at a time. Based on your answers, we will show whether you are likely required to appoint an EU data protection representative.

q1.heading: GDPR in general
q1.title: Is your seat or residence outside the European Economic Area (EEA), for example in Switzerland?
q1.description: Companies also include sole proprietors and entrepreneurs. Organizations also include cooperatives, foundations and associations. Private individuals who do not run a business may also fall under the GDPR. The European Economic Area (EEA) comprises all EU member states as well as the Principality of Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.

q2.heading: Applicability in Switzerland
q2.title: Is your offering also directed at persons in Germany, the Principality of Liechtenstein or other EEA countries, including free offerings?
q2.description: Offering means all services and goods. It does not matter whether an offering is paid or free. The offering may include, for example, free e-books, newsletters or white papers for recipients in Germany and elsewhere in the EEA. Intent is sufficient — actual success of the offering is not decisive. Indicators include shipping to persons in the EEA, advertising aimed at persons in the EEA, use of EEA-related top-level domains (TLDs) such as .at, .de, .eu or .li, mention of customers in the EEA, or use of EEA-related languages and currencies.

q3.heading: Representation in EU
q3.title: Do you monitor the behavior of people in Germany, the Principality of Liechtenstein and other EEA countries, for example by tracking app users or website visitors?
q3.description: Monitoring includes, among other things, tracking app users or website visitors from the EEA to trace internet activity, determine personal preferences or predict possible behavior. Examples include tracking for personalized advertising with Google Ads or reach measurement with Google Analytics. The use of cookies, fingerprinting or geolocation as well as conducting surveys may also constitute behavioral monitoring.

contentAndUse.label: Content and use of generated privacy policies

q1.question: May I publish the generated privacy policy on my website?
q1.answer: Yes. The generated privacy policy is intended to be published on your website and linked from your cookie banner, footer, or legal notice where appropriate.

q2.question: Do I need to adapt the privacy policy?
q2.answer: You should review the generated text carefully and adjust it where your actual processing activities differ from the questionnaire answers or scan results.

q3.question: Does the privacy policy also cover social media profiles?
q3.answer: The generator focuses on your website. Separate privacy information may be required for social media pages or third-party platforms.

q4.question: What happens when my website changes?
q4.answer: If you add new tools, trackers, or data processing activities, you should update your privacy policy accordingly and regenerate or revise it.

q5.question: Can I use the privacy policy in multiple languages?
q5.answer: You can create and maintain separate language versions. Make sure each version accurately reflects the same processing activities.

q6.question: Who is responsible for the content of the privacy policy?
q6.answer: You remain responsible as the controller. The generator provides a draft based on your inputs; it does not replace legal advice.

q7.question: How does the website scan work?
q7.answer: We analyse publicly accessible elements of your website to detect common tools, embeds, trackers, and services that should be reflected in your privacy policy.

q8.question: What data is processed during the scan?
q8.answer: The scan uses the URL you provide and analyses publicly available website content. No visitor data from your website is collected for the scan itself.

q9.question: Do I have to answer questions that do not apply to me?
q9.answer: Answer the questionnaire as accurately as possible. If a topic does not apply, select the option that best reflects your situation so the draft stays correct.

q10.question: Can I use the generator more than once?
q10.answer: Yes. You can run a new scan and generate an updated privacy policy whenever your website or processing activities change.

q11.question: How much does the privacy policy generator cost?
q11.answer: Pricing depends on the selected plan and any add-ons such as EU representation. The current prices are shown before checkout.

q12.question: How can I pay?
q12.answer: Payment is handled securely during checkout. Available payment methods are shown on the order page.

q13.question: Can I cancel my subscription?
q13.answer: Subscription terms and cancellation options depend on your plan. Please refer to our terms of service or contact support for details.

q14.question: Will I receive help if I have questions?
q14.answer: Yes. Our support team can help with questions about using the generator and your generated documents.

q15.question: Does Datenschutzpartner provide legal advice?
q15.answer: The generator produces a draft based on your inputs. Individual legal advice is available separately where needed.

q16.question: How do I contact support?
q16.answer: Use our contact form or reach out via the support options listed on the website. We aim to respond as quickly as possible.
